prose.summary: A copywriter turns a product, a feature, or a half-formed pitch from a founder into sentences that get someone to click, buy, or read the next line. The role next to it people confuse it with is content strategist: strategists plan what gets said and where, copywriters write the words that go on the page. Most of the job lives inside a doc or a Figma comment thread, not a content calendar.
prose.day_to_day: Mornings usually start with opening whatever is already in progress: an email sequence half-drafted, a landing page with three headline options stacked in a comment thread, a Slack message from someone in growth asking for '5 subject lines by noon.' A good chunk of the week goes to writing alone with a brief and a deadline, but the rest is meetings: a call with design to see how copy sits in the layout, a review with a manager who wants the second paragraph cut, sometimes a session with legal because a claim needs softening. The moment people look forward to is seeing a draft come back from review with almost nothing touched, or watching an A/B test confirm the version you fought for. There's also the unglamorous stretch: rewriting the same CTA nine ways because the client can't articulate what's wrong with the first eight. By Friday there's usually one piece that shipped clean and one that's still stuck in someone's inbox waiting on approval.
prose.work_environment: Most of this work happens at a desk, alone, with headphones on, which is part of why the remote share sits above half: writing doesn't require anyone else in the room, only a shared doc and a Slack channel. Deadlines cluster around launches and campaign dates rather than a steady drip, so a bad week is usually a product launch, a rebrand, or three clients wanting final copy on the same Thursday. Hours are generally normal business hours, but agency-side work can spike hard right before a pitch. Travel is rare; the social part of the job happens over video calls and comment threads rather than in person.
prose.getting_in: There's no license here, and while 7 of postings state a degree requirement, 4 mark it preferred rather than mandatory and 2 explicitly waive it, so a strong portfolio substitutes for credentials in a meaningful share of listings. The realistic path is: build a portfolio of 5 to 8 pieces (landing pages, email sequences, a case study) over 2 to 3 months, often written speculatively for real or invented brands, then take freelance or junior in-house work to get to the experience median of 3 years that 55% of postings state outright. The longest stretch is usually those first 3 years, not because the writing is hard to learn but because agencies and brands want to see it applied to a real business problem, not just a nice sentence. Most people stall right after the portfolio is built, applying broadly without tailoring samples to the specific industry (SaaS copy reads differently from DTC copy, and hiring managers notice).
prose.ladder: Early on you're handed a format (an email, a product page) and a brief, and your job is to execute it well. The step up is being handed a problem instead of a format: 'conversion on this page is flat, fix it,' with no one telling you whether that means a new headline or a new offer. That shift usually happens around year 2 to 3 and requires showing you can read data, not just write clean sentences (which is likely why data-analysis shows up in 17% of postings). Past that, the ladder forks: staying hands-on as a senior or principal copywriter who owns the highest-stakes copy, or moving into content strategy or marketing management where you're briefing other writers instead of drafting yourself. The fork usually happens within 3 to 5 years of starting.
prose.suits: People who like this job tend to enjoy the puzzle of fitting a whole argument into one sentence, and they get a real charge out of hearing that a subject line moved the open rate or that a landing page rewrite dropped bounce. It suits someone comfortable being edited hard and often, since first drafts rarely survive intact. People who leave are usually the ones who wanted to originate ideas and found themselves executing someone else's strategy instead; they tend to drift toward content strategy or brand work where they set the direction rather than fill in the brief. If you need to see your byline to feel the work mattered, this job will frustrate you: most of what you write goes out under a brand's name, not yours.
prose.misconceptions: Outsiders assume copywriting is mostly clever wordplay, taglines and puns, when most paid work is unglamorous: email subject lines, product descriptions, onboarding flows, the small connective sentences nobody notices unless they're wrong. People also assume it's a solitary, purely creative job, but 30% of postings ask for SEO and another 30% for content marketing skill, meaning most copywriters spend real time thinking about keywords and funnels, not just voice.
prose.who_qualifies: Content strategists carry the highest overlap (71% match) since they've already done the writing, just with more planning layered on top; the shift back to pure copywriting is mostly about tightening scope. Marketing managers (54%) and growth marketers (53%) also transfer well, bringing funnel and CRM fluency that copywriting jobs increasingly ask for, though they sometimes have to relearn writing at the sentence level after years of managing others' output. Social media managers (50%) carry over tone and brevity but often need to build range for longer-form formats like email sequences or landing pages.
prose.what_the_numbers_miss: None of this shows what it feels like to have a headline you're proud of killed in a two-minute Slack thread by someone who's never written one, or the particular relief of a client saying 'this is exactly it' on the first try. It also can't capture how much of the job is translating a founder's vague sense of 'make it pop' into something specific enough to write.

steps.how: Pick a format mix: a landing page, an email sequence, a product description set, a case study. Write them for real companies (unsolicited) or invented ones, spending 2 to 3 months total. You're done when each piece could survive a stranger asking 'why this word, why here.'

Pitch a small brand, newsletter, or local business directly, or take a freelance gig on a platform that pays. This usually takes 2 to 6 weeks of pitching to land. The goal isn't the fee, it's having one piece you can point to that a stranger paid for.

Spend 2 to 3 weeks going through a free SEO course and setting up a trial account in a CRM tool (email sequences, list segmentation). These show up in 30% and 19% of postings respectively, and even basic fluency separates you from portfolio-only applicants.

steps.do: Apply to junior or freelance roles
steps.how: Target postings that don't gate on the 3-year experience median, usually junior copywriter, marketing associate, or in-house freelance roles. Expect this stage to take 3 to 6 months of applying and interviewing before landing something steady.

Once you have a year of applied work, pick a lane (SaaS, DTC email, B2B) based on what you enjoyed and what paid best. This is less a step with an end date and more a decision that shapes which senior roles open up around year 3.

prose.tools: The real gatekeepers are plain writing and editing tools (Google Docs, Notion) plus whatever CRM the employer runs on for email sequences, since 19% of postings ask for CRM fluency directly. SEO tools (Ahrefs, SurferSEO type platforms) show up often enough (30%) that basic comfort with keyword research is close to expected, not optional. Design tools like Figma are nice to have for seeing how copy sits in layout, but they're rarely a hard requirement. Postings increasingly mention data analysis (17%), suggesting comfort reading A/B test results is becoming part of the baseline rather than a specialty.

industries.name: SaaS
industries.note: Copy here is dense with feature explanation and onboarding flows; 13% of postings name SaaS specifically, and the work leans heavily on clarity over cleverness.

industries.name: Agency
industries.note: Fastest pace, most format variety, but also the most client churn and rewrite cycles since you're writing for someone else's brand voice, not your own company's.

industries.name: B2B
industries.note: Longer sales cycles mean more whitepapers, case studies and email nurture sequences than punchy one-liners; shows up in 15% of postings.

industries.name: Consumer brand / DTC
industries.note: Highest volume of short-form work (product pages, social captions, ad copy) and the tightest feedback loop between what you write and what sells.

specializations.name: Email and CRM copywriting
specializations.why: 19% of postings ask for CRM skill directly and email remains one of the highest-ROI channels brands measure, so writers who can build full lifecycle sequences (not just one-off blasts) get paid more and hired faster.

specializations.name: SEO content copywriting
specializations.why: 30% of postings mention SEO; writers who understand search intent and can write for both ranking and conversion are harder to find than generalist writers, and it's a skill that ages well as search itself changes.

specializations.name: B2B SaaS messaging
specializations.why: SaaS companies pay well for writers who can make a technical product sound simple without dumbing it down, and 13% of postings name SaaS specifically as the domain, often paying above the median for the skill.

pros: There's a specific, small satisfaction in watching a headline you argued for beat the client's original in an A/B test.
The work is portable: a laptop and a doc are the whole toolkit, which is part of why over half these roles are remote.
You get to see the direct effect of your sentences on a real number (open rate, conversion, signups) more often than in most writing jobs.
The variety of format (email one day, landing page the next, a product description the day after) keeps the work from going stale the way a single long-form beat can.
cons: Your best line often gets cut for a legal or brand reason that has nothing to do with whether it worked.
A lot of the job is rewriting the same idea eight different ways because a stakeholder can't say precisely what's bothering them about draft one.
The byline rarely has your name on it, so career proof depends on a portfolio you have to maintain yourself, not on public credit.
Deadlines cluster around launches, so slow weeks can flip into three overlapping deadlines with no warning.

faq.q: how long does it take to become a copywriter
faq.a: Most people spend 2 to 3 months building a spec portfolio, then 3 to 6 months applying before landing a paid junior or freelance role. Reaching the experience level most job postings ask for (a median of 3 years) takes longer, but you're working and paid the whole time.

faq.q: do you need a degree to be a copywriter
faq.a: No, not strictly: while 7 of measured postings mention a degree, 2 explicitly waive it and a portfolio of real writing samples generally matters more than the credential itself. What employers check first is whether your samples fit the kind of copy they need (SaaS, DTC, B2B all read differently).

faq.q: copywriter vs content strategist, what's the difference
faq.a: A copywriter writes the actual sentences that go on the page; a content strategist decides what gets written, in what order, and why. The overlap is real (71% of content strategists could move into copywriting with minimal retraining) but the day-to-day differs: one is mostly drafting, the other is mostly planning.

Yes, and it usually is: 55% of measured openings are remote, since the core task (writing in a shared doc) doesn't require being in an office. Agency roles sometimes want in-person time around big pitches, but that's the exception rather than the rule.

faq.q: is copywriting at risk from AI
faq.a: The measurements can't answer that directly, but the skill mix in current postings (SEO, data analysis, CRM strategy alongside writing) suggests employers are hiring for judgment about what to say and to whom, not just sentence production. The writers most exposed are likely those doing high-volume, low-context copy with no strategic layer attached.
